Title: Cache-Aside pattern example introduces silent race condition without atomic invalidation/leasing
Description: The lesson demonstrates the standard Cache-Aside pattern (Read: check cache -> DB -> write cache; Write: write DB -> delete cache) but omits the critical concurrency window where a slow concurrent read can re-populate the cache with stale data after an update has executed. It lacks discussion of mutex locks, leases (e.g., Gutter/Memcached lease tokens), or version timestamps.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/caching.
2. Scroll down to 'Cache Invalidation Patterns: Cache-Aside'.
3. Review the code example and accompanying sequence diagram.
4. Observe that concurrent Read/Write race is unaddressed and marked as '100% consistent'.
Expected_Result: The lesson should clearly explain that Cache-Aside provides eventual consistency, explain the stale read-after-write edge case, and introduce mitigation techniques (short TTLs, cache lease tokens, dual writes with versioning, or CDC via Debezium).
Actual_Result: Cache-Aside is presented as a universally consistent pattern without discussing race conditions or stale cache overwrites during high concurrency.
Impact: Students learning system design will implement flawed caching tiers that lead to silent data corruption in high-concurrency production systems.
Evidence: Snippet on /academy/caching states: 'Deleting the cache key on write guarantees your users will always see fresh data from the database on their next query.'
Screenshot_Reference: N/A - Audited from DOM text & diagram
Technical_Reason: In high QPS environments: Thread A reads DB (val=1), Thread B writes DB (val=2) and evicts cache, Thread A writes stale (val=1) back to cache with no TTL or long TTL.
Suggested_Fix: Update the curriculum text and sequence diagram to explicitly illustrate the race condition, explain why absolute cache-DB consistency is impossible without distributed locks, and detail mitigation patterns (singleflight, leases, TTLs).

Title: Oversimplified 'Pick Any Two' CAP Theorem representation misleads architectural trade-offs
Description: The lesson presents the classic 2-of-3 triangle ('Pick 2: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance') implying that 'CA' (Consistency + Availability without Partition Tolerance) is a valid distributed system design option. In real-world networks, network partitions are inevitable physical realities; a distributed system can only choose between CP and AP during a network partition.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/distributed-systems.
2. Scroll to 'The CAP Theorem'.
3. Inspect the 2-of-3 Venn/Triangle graphic and accompanying explanation.
Expected_Result: The lesson should clarify that Partition Tolerance (P) is mandatory for any distributed system across a network. When a partition occurs, the system must trade off between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP). It should also introduce the PACELC theorem (Else: Latency vs Consistency during normal operation).
Actual_Result: The text states: 'You can choose to build a CA system if you don't need network partition tolerance, such as in single-cluster RDBMS.'
Impact: Fails standard engineering interview expectations; misleads engineers into thinking network partitions are optional configurations.
Evidence: Text excerpt: 'CAP Theorem: Choose any two from Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.'
Technical_Reason: Network partitions (cable cuts, switch failures, GC pauses) cannot be avoided in distributed systems. A single-node RDBMS is not a distributed system and therefore CAP theorem does not apply to it.
Suggested_Fix: Refactor the CAP theorem section: explain that P is non-negotiable in distributed environments, frame the decision as CP vs AP under network fault conditions, and add the PACELC extension for normal operating states.

Title: Redis rate limiter code example uses separate GET and INCR/EXPIRE calls instead of atomic Lua script
Description: In the Distributed Rate Limiting section, the Python/Node code example executes a separate GET, conditional check, and INCR/EXPIRE against Redis without using an atomic Lua script (`EVAL`) or Redis pipeline/multi-exec, creating a classic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition allowing traffic bursts to exceed configured quotas.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/rate-limiting.
2. Scroll to 'Distributed Rate Limiting Implementation'.
3. Review the code sample showing `val = redis.get(key); if val < limit: redis.incr(key); redis.expire(key, 60)`.
Expected_Result: The implementation must use an atomic Redis Lua script or explain why non-atomic multi-roundtrip checks fail under concurrent request spikes.
Actual_Result: Non-atomic multi-step Redis calls are presented as production-grade distributed rate limiting.
Impact: High-throughput services using this snippet will suffer rate limiter bypasses and race conditions during traffic spikes.
Evidence: Non-atomic sequence in code block: separate `GET`, `IF`, `INCR`, `EXPIRE` commands.
Technical_Reason: Multiple concurrent worker threads or servers will all read `val < limit` simultaneously before any has incremented it, allowing N concurrent requests to pass through.
Suggested_Fix: Provide a production-ready Lua script (`redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]); if ... then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end`) and explain atomic script execution on single-threaded Redis engine.
Notes: Affects code correctness and architectural rigor.

Title: Dragging canvas nodes on touch viewports triggers unintended page scroll and misaligns connection edges
Description: On touch-enabled viewports (Mobile & Tablet), attempting to drag architectural nodes (e.g., Client, Load Balancer, PostgreSQL) on the canvas causes the browser viewport to scroll simultaneously due to missing `touch-action: none` on the canvas container, resulting in misplaced connectors and broken SVG bezier curve edges.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Open /builder on a mobile viewport (375x812 or 768x1024).
2. Attempt to drag a node from the sidebar onto the canvas or move an existing node.
3. Observe page scrolls vertically while dragging, and connector anchor coordinates become offset.
Expected_Result: Canvas should capture touch events exclusively with `touch-action: none` / `e.preventDefault()`, allowing smooth node dragging without viewport scrolling.
Actual_Result: Page scrolls erratically and edge coordinates become disconnected from node handles.
Impact: Interactive Builder is virtually unusable on mobile and tablet touch devices.
Evidence: Missing CSS rule `touch-action: none` on `.builder-canvas` DOM element.
Screenshot_Reference: N/A - Audited via DOM & viewport simulation
Technical_Reason: Default touch event propagation is not intercepted by the canvas event handlers.
Suggested_Fix: Apply `touch-action: none` to the canvas container and handle PointerEvents API (`pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`) with proper coordinate normalization via `getBoundingClientRect()`.
Notes: Affects mobile usability of core interactive tool.

Title: Course progress count does not synchronize across tabs or persist reliably on hard reload in private browsing
Description: Marking lessons as complete updates local React state but does not dispatch a `storage` event or robustly validate fallback storage when LocalStorage access is restricted or when navigating across multiple tabs, causing the header progress badge (e.g., '0/18 shipped') to revert to 0 on hard refresh.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Open /academy.
2. Navigate to '01 Capacity Estimation' and click 'Mark as Complete'.
3. Observe progress updates to '1/18'.
4. Open a second tab to /academy or perform a hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R).
5. Check header progress counter.
Expected_Result: Completed state should reliably persist in LocalStorage, sync across open tabs via `window.addEventListener('storage', ...)`, and reflect accurately on refresh.
Actual_Result: Progress state reverts to 0 or becomes desynchronized between tabs.
Impact: Learners lose motivation and track of curriculum completion progress.
Evidence: LocalStorage hydration hook lacks storage change listener and error boundary fallback.
Technical_Reason: React state initialized from default 0 before LocalStorage hydration completes without SSR/CSR hydration reconciliation.
Suggested_Fix: Implement a custom hook `useLocalStorage` with proper SSR hydration check (`useEffect`), cross-tab `window.addEventListener('storage')` listener, and in-memory fallback for restricted environments.

Title: Theme toggle button and mobile hamburger trigger lack accessible name (aria-label)
Description: The Theme Toggle icon button (Sun/Moon) and the Mobile Hamburger Menu trigger button are rendered as `<button>` elements containing only inline SVG icons with no `aria-label`, `aria-expanded`, or inner text, rendering them unannounced to screen reader users (e.g., NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS).
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Inspect the DOM of the top navigation header on / or /academy.
2. Locate the theme toggle `<button>` and mobile menu `<button>`.
3. Check for `aria-label`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-expanded`, or visually hidden text.
Expected_Result: Buttons should have descriptive labels: `aria-label='Toggle dark mode'` and `aria-label='Open navigation menu'` with `aria-expanded='false|true'`.
Actual_Result: Elements are rendered as `<button class='...'><svg>...</svg></button>` with an accessible name of empty string.
Impact: Screen reader users cannot identify the purpose of key interface controls.
Evidence: DOM inspection: `<button class='p-2 rounded-lg ...'><svg ...></svg></button>` without `aria-label` attribute.
Technical_Reason: Icon-only buttons missing `aria-label` or `<span class='sr-only'>` child elements.
Suggested_Fix: Add `aria-label='Toggle dark theme'` and `aria-label='Toggle navigation menu'` with dynamic `aria-expanded` attributes on all icon buttons.

Description: On mobile viewports with width <= 390px, the multi-column layout for the System Simulator (Traffic Generator, Server Pool, Queue Depth, Latency Histogram) does not collapse to a single column, generating horizontal scrollbars (`overflow-x: scroll`) and clipping real-time SVG charts.

2. Observe the grid layout containing the RPS slider, node status cards, and latency chart.
3. Attempt to view the latency histogram without scrolling horizontally.
Expected_Result: Layout should wrap into a clean single-column stack (`grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4`) with charts auto-resizing via `width: 100%; height: auto`.
Actual_Result: Fixed-width min-width containers force horizontal scrolling and truncate axis labels on mobile.

Title: Kafka Exactly-Once Semantics explanation conflates idempotent producer with end-to-end exactly-once delivery
Description: The lesson asserts that setting `enable.idempotence=true` and `acks=all` on the Kafka producer guarantees 'end-to-end exactly-once processing across the entire distributed system'. In reality, producer idempotence only prevents duplicates within a single producer session to the broker partition; end-to-end EOS requires Kafka transactional API (`sendOffsetsToTransaction`) across read-process-write streams and idempotent consumer downstream database writes (upserts / deduplication IDs).
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/kafka.
2. Scroll to 'Message Delivery Guarantees: Exactly-Once'.
3. Read the description of `enable.idempotence`.
Expected_Result: The lesson should clearly distinguish between at-least-once, at-most-once, producer idempotence, transactional Kafka streams, and end-to-end consumer idempotency (e.g. unique constraint / DB upsert / Outbox pattern).
Actual_Result: Text incorrectly claims producer config alone provides complete end-to-end exactly-once processing.
Impact: Engineers will design message consumer architectures without necessary idempotency keys, leading to duplicate side effects (e.g., duplicate payments or emails).
Evidence: Text claim: 'Kafka achieves true end-to-end exactly-once delivery simply by enabling producer idempotence.'
Technical_Reason: Producer idempotence uses sequence numbers per PID (Producer ID) and partition. Consumer failures during DB writes require application-level idempotency.
Suggested_Fix: Revise the explanation to detail the end-to-end requirements for EOS: transactional read-process-write loops and downstream consumer idempotency mechanisms.
Notes: Critical nuance in distributed streaming architectures.

Section: Step 3: Base62 Encoding vs Hash Collisions
Title: URL shortener lab suggests MD5 hashing without addressing inevitable birthday paradox collisions
Description: In Step 3 of the URL Shortener lab, the guide presents taking the first 7 characters of an `MD5(long_url)` hash as a primary encoding strategy. However, truncation to 7 base62 characters from a 128-bit hash causes massive collision rates under the Birthday Paradox after only ~100k URLs. The lab does not provide collision detection/retry logic or highlight why counter/Snowflake ID generation with Base62 encoding is the industry standard.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/labs/url-shortener.
2. Scroll to 'Step 3: Generating the Short URL Hash'.
3. Review the code snippet and trade-off table.
Expected_Result: The lab should prioritize distributed counter / Snowflake ID generation with Base62 conversion (zero collision guarantee), and show the collision resolution loop if hash truncation is used.
Actual_Result: Truncated MD5 hash is presented as a primary solution without collision handling code or mathematical risk analysis.
Impact: Students implement production URL shorteners that silently overwrite existing redirect mappings when hash collisions occur.
Evidence: Snippet: `short_url = base62_encode(md5(long_url))[:7]` without database collision check or sequence generator.
Technical_Reason: 7 Base62 characters = 62^7 = 3.52 trillion combinations. But truncating an MD5 hash without unique counter input yields birthday collisions at p > 0.01 at only ~260,000 items.
Suggested_Fix: Restructure Step 3 to show Twitter Snowflake / DB Sequence -> Base62 encoding as primary approach; contrast with hash-based approach and provide collision-checking DB query loop.
Notes: Standard system design interview case study.

Title: Copy Code' buttons lack visible focus outline and screen reader notification when code is copied
Description: The 'Copy' button located in the upper-right corner of code blocks has `outline: none` without a custom focus ring (`focus-visible:ring-2`), and clicking it only updates an icon without triggering an `aria-live='polite'` announcement (e.g., 'Code copied to clipboard').
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/capacity-estimation.
2. Use the 'Tab' key to navigate to a code block copy button.
3. Press Enter or Space to activate it.
Expected_Result: A clear, visible focus outline should appear when focused via keyboard. When triggered, a screen reader should announce 'Copied to clipboard' via an `aria-live` region.
Actual_Result: No visible outline is displayed on focus, and no assistive audio confirmation is announced upon copying.
Impact: Keyboard-only and screen reader users cannot tell when the copy button is focused or whether the copy action succeeded.
Evidence: Button styling lacks `:focus-visible` styles; missing `aria-live` container.
Screenshot_Reference: N/A - Audited from DOM and focus behavior
Technical_Reason: CSS reset removes outline without replacement focus indicator; state change not wired to ARIA live region.
Suggested_Fix: Add `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-indigo-500 focus-visible:outline-none` and a hidden `aria-live='polite'` status element.
Notes: WCAG 2.1 AA Focus Visible (2.4.7) & Status Messages (4.1.3).

Subcategory: Diagram Clipping & Contrast in Light Theme
Title: Consistent Hashing ring node labels have low contrast in light mode and overlap at smaller tablet widths
Description: In the Load Balancers lesson, the SVG diagram illustrating virtual nodes on a hash ring uses light-gray text (`#94A3B8`) for server labels which fails WCAG AA 4.5:1 contrast against the white background in light mode (measured contrast ratio 2.3:1). Furthermore, at 768px tablet width, the node text overlaps the circular ring border.

2. Navigate to /academy/load-balancers.
3. Scroll down to 'Consistent Hashing: The Hash Ring'.
4. Inspect the text colors of node labels ('Server A', 'Virtual Node A1', etc.) on a 768px viewport.
Expected_Result: Labels should have high contrast (minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio against light backgrounds) and maintain a clean margin around the ring without overlapping text.
Actual_Result: Light gray text is washed out and node label bounding boxes overlap circular SVG path.
Impact: Students in light mode experience eye strain; diagram becomes illegible on tablet screens.
Evidence: Computed text color `#94a3b8` on `#ffffff` background = 2.31:1 contrast ratio.

Title: Search input lacks clear button and does not provide an accessible 'No results found' empty state
Description: When searching for curriculum topics (e.g. 'Kubernetes', 'Sharding', or non-matching query 'xyz123'), typing into the search bar provides no quick 'Clear' (X) button to reset the search string, and typing an unmatched string causes the module list to collapse completely without displaying an informative empty state message.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to https://system-design-orpin.vercel.app/academy.
2. In the curriculum search bar, type 'xyz999'.
3. Observe the curriculum list area.
Expected_Result: A clear 'No lessons found matching "xyz999"' message should appear with a 'Clear filter' button, alongside an inline 'X' clear icon inside the input.
Actual_Result: Curriculum cards disappear completely leaving a blank gap with no feedback.
Impact: Users may assume the page failed to render or crashed.
Evidence: Searching unmatched term results in empty container without empty state component.

Suggested_Fix: Render a dedicated `<NoResults query={searchQuery} onClear={resetSearch} />` component when `filteredModules.length === 0` and add a clear button to the search input.

Title: Database sharding section glosses over cross-shard joins, distributed transactions, and re-sharding complexity
Description: The lesson advises sharding databases by `user_id` when single-node write capacity is exceeded, but fails to explain the severe architectural consequences: loss of cross-shard foreign keys/joins, cross-shard ACID transactions (requiring 2PC or Saga), and the operational nightmare of re-sharding when a single shard grows unevenly (hot shard problem).
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/scaling-to-millions.
2. Scroll to 'Step 6: Database Sharding'.
3. Read the pros and cons of sharding.
Expected_Result: The lesson must detail practical solutions for cross-shard queries (denormalization, application-level joins, global secondary indices, distributed SQL like CockroachDB/Yugabyte) and strategies for handling celebrity / hot partition keys.
Actual_Result: The text states sharding simply 'splits data across multiple machines' without discussing distributed query penalties or re-sharding rebalancing protocols.
Impact: Underprepares engineers for real-world distributed database migration pitfalls and staff-level interview follow-ups.
Evidence: Brief 2-paragraph overview without mentioning cross-shard transactions or re-sharding overhead.
Technical_Reason: Oversimplification of one of the hardest problems in distributed stateful systems.
Suggested_Fix: Add a dedicated subsection on 'The Hidden Costs of Sharding': Cross-shard joins, Distributed Transactions & 2PC overhead, Re-sharding / Consistent Hashing migration, and Hot Shard mitigation.

Title: Simulation engine continues running active requestAnimationFrame animation loop when browser tab is in background
Description: The simulation engine on `/simulator` uses a `setInterval` / `requestAnimationFrame` loop to generate simulated traffic packets and update canvas metrics, but lacks `document.visibilityState` listening. When the user switches to another tab, the simulation loop continues full throttle, causing unnecessary CPU cycles and battery drain on mobile/laptop devices.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Open /simulator and start simulation.
2. Open browser Task Manager.
3. Switch to another browser tab for 2 minutes.
4. Check CPU usage and simulation state accumulation.
Expected_Result: Simulation loop should automatically pause when `document.hidden === true` and resume when the tab becomes visible again.
Actual_Result: Simulation continues executing high-frequency state updates in background.
Impact: Excessive CPU and battery consumption on client devices; accumulated state can cause frame drops upon returning to tab.
Evidence: Missing `visibilitychange` event listener in simulator component lifecycle.
Screenshot_Reference: N/A - Audited via component lifecycle code
Technical_Reason: Timer loops not decoupled or paused when `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`.
Suggested_Fix: Add a `useEffect` hook listening to `document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', handleVisibilityChange)` to automatically freeze simulation ticks when tab is unfocused.

Title: External resource links targeting new tabs omit `rel='noopener noreferrer'` attribute
Description: External reference links in the lesson content and footer that open in a new tab (`target='_blank'`) are missing the `rel='noopener noreferrer'` attribute, exposing the application to reverse tabnabbing vulnerability where malicious third-party destinations can manipulate `window.opener.location`.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Inspect external documentation links in lesson footers and lab resources.
2. Check the `rel` attribute on `<a target='_blank' ...>` elements.
Expected_Result: All external links with `target='_blank'` should include `rel='noopener noreferrer'`.
Actual_Result: Some anchor tags contain only `target='_blank'` without explicit `rel` attribute.
Impact: Security hygiene vulnerability allowing potential phishing or redirect manipulation via `window.opener`.
Evidence: DOM elements: `<a href='https://...' target='_blank'>` missing `rel` attribute.
Technical_Reason: Standard React JSX anchor tags without centralized SafeLink wrapper component.
Suggested_Fix: Create an external link wrapper component that automatically injects `rel='noopener noreferrer'` for all external URLs.

Title: Inconsistent difficulty classifications and time estimate units across curriculum cards
Description: Across different curriculum cards, difficulty levels fluctuate between inconsistent taxonomies: some use 'Beginner / Intermediate / Advanced', others use 'Level 0 - 8', and others use 'Easy / Medium / Hard'. Similarly, time estimates inconsistently mix '15 mins', '20m', '0.5 hrs', and missing estimate labels.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy.
2. Compare badges across '01 How the Internet Works', '01 Capacity Estimation', '01 Distributed Systems', and '01 Docker'.
Expected_Result: Standardized badge hierarchy across all lessons: Consistent Difficulty (`Beginner` | `Intermediate` | `Advanced`) and standardized time format (e.g. `15 min read`).
Actual_Result: Mixed casing ('Beginner', 'easy', 'ADVANCED'), mixed time formatting ('15m', '25 mins', '1 hour').
Impact: Reduces visual professionalism and creates learner confusion regarding curriculum progression.
Evidence: Curriculum card props have unvalidated freeform string types.
Technical_Reason: Lack of TypeScript enum or strict schema for lesson metadata.
Suggested_Fix: Define a strict TypeScript type `type Difficulty = 'Beginner' | 'Intermediate' | 'Advanced'` and format all estimated durations through a single helper function `formatDuration(minutes: number): string`.

Title: Circuit Breaker state transition diagram omits Half-Open state concurrency throttling
Description: The state machine for the Circuit Breaker pattern illustrates transitions between CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF-OPEN, but describes HALF-OPEN as 'allowing requests to pass through normally to test the downstream service'. In reality, allowing all requests through in HALF-OPEN will immediately re-overwhelm a recovering service. A robust circuit breaker must throttle HALF-OPEN traffic to a single trial probe request or a very small percentage (e.g. 5%) of traffic.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/failure-engineering.
2. Scroll to 'The Circuit Breaker Pattern'.
3. Review the Half-Open state explanation and transition diagram.
Expected_Result: The explanation and diagram should specify that HALF-OPEN permits only a limited, metered number of probe requests (trial calls) to evaluate downstream health before transitioning back to CLOSED.
Actual_Result: Text claims: 'In Half-Open state, the breaker lets requests through to see if the service has recovered.'
Impact: Engineers implementing circuit breakers from this guide will cause thundering herd outages on recovering microservices.
Evidence: Missing rate-limited probe explanation in Half-Open state definition.
Technical_Reason: Omission of the concurrency limit / canary trial mechanism in Half-Open state logic.
Suggested_Fix: Update the state machine diagram and text to highlight that Half-Open executes a rate-limited canary trial probe before transitioning to Closed upon consecutive successes.

Title: Lessons lack interactive self-assessment quizzes or scenario-based checks to validate learning comprehension
Description: While the platform provides excellent reading content and labs, individual lesson pages currently end abruptly with navigation links without any interactive micro-quizzes, flashcard concept checks, or architectural scenario questions to test student comprehension before advancing to the next module.

2. Scroll to the bottom of the lesson.
3. Note absence of interactive knowledge verification questions.
Expected_Result: Each lesson should conclude with 2-3 interactive multiple-choice or scenario questions (e.g. 'When should you choose L4 over L7 load balancing?') with immediate feedback and answer explanations.
Actual_Result: No interactive knowledge checks are present on lesson pages.
Impact: Decreases active recall, concept retention, and engagement for interview preparation students.
Evidence: Lesson footer terminates directly into 'Next Lesson' CTA without review component.
Technical_Reason: Interactive quiz components not yet authored or integrated into the markdown/MDX lesson renderer.
Suggested_Fix: Introduce an `<InteractiveQuiz questions={...} />` component at the bottom of each lesson module.

Title: Brand logo icon and title text have subtle 1px vertical misalignment on Safari/WebKit rendering engine
Description: In Safari and WebKit-based browsers, the SVG logo icon in the top left navbar sits 1px higher than the baseline of the 'System Design Academy' typography due to `display: inline-flex` without `items-center` alignment on the parent anchor wrapper.

Title: Transactional Outbox pattern explanation omits CDC (Change Data Capture) log tailing vs polling trade-offs
Description: The lesson introduces the Transactional Outbox pattern as writing to an `outbox` table within the same DB transaction as business logic, but assumes a simple DB polling publisher (`SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published = false`). It fails to discuss the performance bottlenecks of frequent DB polling (table bloat, lock contention) and omits the industry-standard alternative: Transaction log tailing via Change Data Capture (CDC) like Debezium or PostgreSQL WAL replication slots.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /academy/event-driven-architecture.
2. Scroll to 'The Transactional Outbox Pattern'.
3. Review the message relay mechanism description.
Expected_Result: The lesson should contrast DB Polling (simple, but polling latency and DB index contention) with Transaction Log Tailing (Debezium/Kafka Connect reading WAL logs, zero polling overhead, strictly ordered).
Actual_Result: Only polling is mentioned, presenting polling as the only way to read the outbox table.
Impact: Students building outbox pipelines in production will experience heavy database CPU spikes from polling queries under high volume.
Evidence: Text describes a cron job polling the table every few seconds without WAL/CDC discussion.
Technical_Reason: Omission of log miner / WAL replication stream architectures in event streaming.
Suggested_Fix: Add a dedicated comparison subsection: 'Polling Publisher vs Transaction Log Tailing (CDC / Debezium)' detailing architectural trade-offs.

Title: Dynamic lesson pages share identical generic `<meta name='description'>` and lack Open Graph image tags
Description: All deep lesson routes (e.g. `/academy/docker`, `/academy/kafka`, `/academy/kubernetes`) share a static generic meta description tag ('System Design Academy - Learn scalable architectures') rather than dynamic per-lesson summaries, and omit `og:image` and `twitter:card` tags for social preview card generation.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Inspect HTML `<head>` source code on /academy/docker and /academy/kafka.
2. Check `<title>`, `<meta name='description'>`, and `<meta property='og:image'>`.
Expected_Result: Each page should have a unique dynamic title (e.g. 'Docker for Production - System Design Academy') and specific meta description with an Open Graph social card preview.

Title: Architecture Builder lacks PNG/SVG image export or shareable URL permalink for created diagrams
Description: After building a complete system architecture diagram on `/builder` with custom nodes and connections, users have no option to export the canvas as a PNG/SVG image or generate a shareable URL permalink containing the serialized diagram state.
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Navigate to /builder.
2. Add Client, Load Balancer, Redis, and Postgres nodes.
3. Connect edges.
4. Look for an 'Export as Image' or 'Share Diagram' button in toolbar.
Expected_Result: Toolbar should provide 'Export PNG', 'Export SVG', and 'Copy Share Link' (encoding graph JSON into URL hash/query or saving to backend).
Actual_Result: No export or sharing capability is provided in the toolbar.
Impact: Users cannot save, export, or share their architectural designs for interview practice, team reviews, or resume portfolios.
Evidence: Toolbar features only Reset/Clear without Export actions.
Technical_Reason: Canvas serialization / canvas-to-blob export feature not yet implemented.
Suggested_Fix: Add `html2canvas` or native SVG serialization to allow one-click PNG/SVG download and Base64/compressed URL state sharing.

Component: HTML Heading Elements (H1, H2, H3, H4)
Subcategory: WCAG 2.1 AA - Info and Relationships (1.3.1) & Heading Structure
Title: Heading hierarchy skips levels (e.g. jumping directly from H1 to H3 or H2 to H4)
Description: In several curriculum lessons, subsection headers jump directly from `<h1>` page title to `<h3>` sub-cards without an intervening `<h2>`, or jump from `<h2>` directly to `<h4>`, violating semantic heading order and impairing screen reader document outline navigation (e.g. using the 'H' key in NVDA/VoiceOver).
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Inspect heading elements on /academy/postgres-at-scale.
2. Run an accessibility tree audit on heading levels.
Expected_Result: Heading levels should follow a strict sequential hierarchy (`h1` -> `h2` -> `h3`).
Actual_Result: Document contains skipped levels (`h1` followed directly by `h3` in sidebar and main content).
Impact: Screen reader users navigating by heading levels experience disoriented document hierarchy.
Evidence:
DOM heading structure: `

PostgreSQL at Scale

` followed by `

B-Tree Indexing

`.
Screenshot_Reference: N/A - Audited via DOM tree hierarchy
Technical_Reason: Tailwind utility styling applied directly to arbitrary heading tags without semantic structuring.
Suggested_Fix: Refactor markdown/MDX components to enforce semantic heading tags (`h1` for title, `h2` for main sections, `h3` for subsections) and use CSS classes for visual sizing.

Title: Academy lacks dedicated end-to-end interview case study modules (e.g., Design Netflix, Uber, WhatsApp, Instagram)
Description: While the academy provides outstanding modular primitives (Load Balancers, Caching, Kafka, Postgres, Kubernetes) and hands-on labs, it lacks comprehensive end-to-end system design interview case studies synthesizing all components into holistic architectures (e.g., Design a Real-Time Ride Hailing Service like Uber, Design Video Streaming like Netflix, Design Messenger like WhatsApp, Design Social Feed like Instagram/Twitter).
Steps_to_Reproduce:
1. Review all 8 levels in /academy.
2. Search curriculum for 'Uber', 'Netflix', 'Instagram', 'Twitter', or 'WhatsApp'.
Expected_Result: A dedicated 'Level 9: Real-World Case Studies' containing full end-to-end interview blueprints with requirements, estimations, high-level diagrams, deep-dives, bottlenecks, and failure modes.
Actual_Result: Case studies are only referenced briefly in isolated bullet points without full end-to-end walkthroughs.
Impact: Learners preparing for senior and staff-level FAANG/top-tier system design interviews must look elsewhere for complete full-system architectures.
Evidence: Curriculum index contains building block topics but no comprehensive multi-tier case study chapters.
Technical_Reason: Full case study modules not yet drafted in curriculum content repository.
Suggested_Fix: Add a dedicated section for top 8 classic system design interview problems (URL Shortener, Rate Limiter, Instagram, Twitter/X, Netflix, Uber, WhatsApp, Distributed Web Crawler).
